title: Quiz 1: Machine Learning Fundamentals
description: 120 questions on AI versus machine learning, the three types of learning, classification and regression, clustering with k-means, parameters and hyperparameters, accuracy and the confusion matrix, overfitting, underfitting, bias and variance, and the steps of the machine learning process (with short-answer practice).

questions.question: How are artificial intelligence and machine learning related?
options: Machine learning is one specific approach within the wider field of AI
Artificial intelligence is one specific approach within the wider field of machine learning
Machine learning and artificial intelligence are two names for exactly the same thing
Machine learning replaced artificial intelligence once computers became fast enough
questions.explanation: AI is the overall field or science of making machines behave intelligently. ML is one approach to it, in which the system learns from data instead of following hand-written rules.

questions.question: Which description best fits artificial intelligence as a whole?
options: The practice of storing large amounts of data in one central location for analysis
The field of building systems that perform tasks needing human-like intelligence
The method of fitting a line through a set of points to predict a number
The process of cleaning raw data so that it can be loaded into a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: AI is the broad science. Data storage, line fitting and data cleaning are different activities or individual techniques.

questions.question: What most clearly separates a machine learning system from a traditional program?
options: It runs on special hardware so it can follow the rules a programmer wrote faster
It stores every example it has seen in a lookup table that the programmer wrote by hand
It finds its own rules by learning from examples rather than having them written by hand
It asks a human to approve each answer before the answer is returned to the user
questions.explanation: In traditional programming a person writes the rules. In ML the rules (the model) are learned from data.

questions.question: Every artificial intelligence system uses machine learning.
questions.explanation: ML is one approach to AI. Some AI systems, such as hand-coded rule engines, involve no learning at all.

questions.question: Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence.
questions.explanation: AI is the overall field and ML is a specific approach within it.

questions.question: A team writes thousands of if/else rules by hand so a program can spot spam. Which statement is accurate?
options: It is machine learning, because the program makes decisions automatically on its own
It is machine learning, because thousands of rules are involved in making the decision
It is neither AI nor machine learning, because a person wrote the rules by hand
It is a way of building AI, but it is not machine learning because nothing is learned
questions.explanation: Hand-written rules can still be AI, but ML requires that the system learns the rules from data.

questions.question: In machine learning, what is the 'training data'?
options: The collection of examples the algorithm learns from
The collection of results the finished model produces after deployment
The collection of rules the programmer writes before the algorithm runs
The collection of computers on which the algorithm will be executed
questions.explanation: Training data is the set of examples used to fit the model.

questions.question: What is a 'model' in machine learning?
options: What a data scientist draws: the diagram used to plan the stages of a project
What a training algorithm produces: the learned relationship used to make predictions
What a database stores: the table used to organize the rows of training data
What a programmer writes: the function used to load the files from the disk
questions.explanation: The algorithm trains and the model is the trained result that predicts for new inputs.

questions.question: What is a 'feature' in a dataset used for machine learning?
options: The answer variable that the model is built to predict, such as its sale price
The error value that the model makes when it predicts the wrong answer
An input variable that describes each example, such as a house's floor area
The setting that the engineer picks before the training begins, such as the speed
questions.explanation: Features are the inputs. The thing being predicted is the target (label).

questions.question: What is the 'target variable'?
options: The value the model is given as its input
The value the engineer chooses before training starts
The value that measures how long training took
The value the model is trying to predict
questions.explanation: The target is the output the model learns to predict from the features.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The overall field of making machines act intelligently
An approach to AI in which a system learns from data
An input variable describing each example
The value the model is trained to predict

questions.question: The overall field of making machines behave intelligently is called artificial ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the umbrella field; machine learning is one approach inside it.

questions.question: What defines supervised learning?
options: The training examples come with labels, the 'answers' the model should learn to produce
The training examples come with no labels, so the model looks for structure on its own
The training examples come with a person who watches and corrects the model each time
The training examples come with feedback from an environment that scores each action
questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns from labelled data. No labels means unsupervised; feedback from an environment means reinforcement.

questions.question: What defines unsupervised learning?
options: The data has labels, so the algorithm learns to reproduce the given answers
The data has no labels, so the algorithm looks for structure by itself
The data has a reward signal, so the algorithm learns which actions pay off
The data has been cleaned by a person, so the algorithm needs no extra checks
questions.explanation: Without labels, algorithms such as clustering must discover patterns on their own.

questions.question: What defines reinforcement learning?
options: A model learns from a table of examples that each carry the correct label
A model learns from a pile of examples that have no labels or any feedback
An agent learns from feedback its environment gives in response to its actions
An agent learns from a person who writes out the rules for each situation
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning is driven by feedback (rewards and penalties) from the environment.

questions.question: An email service trains a model on thousands of messages that people already marked as 'spam' or 'not spam'. Which type of learning is this?
options: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
Supervised learning
questions.explanation: The messages carry labels, so the model is learning from the given answers.

questions.question: A retailer feeds purchase histories, with no categories attached, into an algorithm that finds natural groups of shoppers. Which type of learning is this?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
questions.explanation: No labels are given; the algorithm discovers the groups itself.

questions.question: A program learns to play a video game by trying moves and receiving points when it scores. Which type of learning is this?
options: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Clustering analysis
questions.explanation: The score is feedback from the environment, which is the hallmark of reinforcement learning.

questions.question: A robot arm is rewarded each time it places a block on the stack without dropping it. Which type of learning does this describe?
options: Supervised learning, since the reward is a label supplied for each example
Unsupervised learning, since the reward is a group assigned to each example
Reinforcement learning, since the reward is feedback from its environment
Supervised learning, since the robot is a machine that has been programmed
questions.explanation: A reward given for actions taken is environmental feedback, not a label attached to a dataset.

questions.question: Supervised learning needs labelled training data.
questions.explanation: Labels are the 'answers' the model learns to predict.

questions.question: Unsupervised learning uses labelled training data.
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning works with no labels at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is a labelled example?
options: A photo of a cat taken with a phone camera
A folder holding ten thousand unsorted photos
A set of ten thousand pixel values from one photo
A photo of a cat together with the word 'cat'
questions.explanation: A label is the answer attached to an example. An unlabelled photo is just input.

questions.question: Match each type of machine learning to what drives the learning.

pairs.right: Labels (the answers) supplied with the data
Structure found in data with no labels
Feedback from the environment

questions.question: Which type of learning needs somebody to label the data in advance?
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Both unsupervised and reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Labels must be created before supervised training, which is often the expensive part.

questions.question: What does a classification model predict?
options: A number chosen from a continuous range with infinite possibilities
A category chosen from a discrete, fixed set of options
A group chosen from the natural clusters found in unlabelled data
A score chosen from the feedback an environment gives for an action
questions.explanation: Classification has a fixed set of target categories (for example dog or not dog). Regression predicts a continuous value.

questions.question: What does a regression model predict?
options: A discrete category, with only a fixed set of possible results
A cluster number, with only as many results as there are clusters
A continuous numeric value, with infinitely many possible results
A yes or no answer, with exactly two possible results
questions.explanation: Regression targets are continuous, such as a house price or a temperature.

questions.question: Predicting whether a customer will cancel a subscription (yes or no) is which kind of problem?
options: Regression
Clustering
Reinforcement
Classification
questions.explanation: The target is one of a fixed set of categories.

questions.question: Predicting the selling price of a used car from its mileage and age is which kind of problem?
options: Regression
Classification
Clustering
Segmentation
questions.explanation: A price is a continuous value.

questions.question: Predicting tomorrow's rainfall in millimetres is which kind of problem?
options: Classification
Regression
Clustering
Association
questions.explanation: Rainfall in millimetres can take any value in a range, so it is a regression target.

questions.question: Deciding whether a scan shows 'healthy', 'benign' or 'malignant' tissue is which kind of problem?
options: Regression, because there are three possible outputs to choose from
Clustering, because the scan holds three kinds of tissue to be grouped
Classification, because there are three fixed categories
Regression, because the answer can be written with the digits 1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Three fixed categories make it classification, even if they are stored as numbers.

questions.question: Match each task to the kind of supervised learning problem it is.

pairs.right: Regression: the answer is a continuous number

pairs.left: Deciding if a transaction is fraud or not
pairs.right: Binary classification: two fixed categories
Regression: the answer is a price that can take any value

pairs.left: Recognising which of five fruits is in a photo
pairs.right: Multi-class classification: five fixed categories

questions.question: Which of these algorithms is used for classification?
options: k-means clustering
Linear regression
Principal components
k-nearest neighbours (kNN)
questions.explanation: kNN, decision trees, random forests and neural nets can all classify. k-means is unsupervised, and linear regression predicts numbers.

questions.question: Which pair lists two algorithms that can be used for classification?
options: Decision tree and random forest
Decision tree and k-means
Random forest and linear regression
k-means and linear regression
questions.explanation: Decision trees and random forests classify. k-means is clustering, and linear regression is a regression method.

questions.question: Which algorithm is used to predict a continuous number such as a house price?
options: Logistic regression
Linear regression
k-means
k-nearest neighbours as a classifier
questions.explanation: Linear regression predicts continuous values.

questions.question: Despite its name, logistic regression is almost always used for what?
options: Predicting a continuous number, such as a price
Grouping unlabelled data into clusters
Binary classification, such as yes or no
Learning from rewards in a game
questions.explanation: Logistic regression outputs a probability that is turned into one of two classes.

questions.question: Logistic regression is mainly used to predict continuous values such as prices.
questions.explanation: It is almost always used for binary classification. Linear regression is the continuous-value method.

questions.question: A model that predicts whether an email is spam is solving a regression problem.
questions.explanation: Spam or not spam is two fixed categories, so it is classification.

questions.question: Which statement about kNN is correct?
options: It groups unlabelled examples by moving cluster centres until they settle
It fits a straight line through the examples and reads off the answer from it
It learns by being rewarded when an action leads to a good outcome
It classifies a new example by looking at the labels of its closest training examples
questions.explanation: kNN is a supervised classification method: the class of a new point comes from its k nearest labelled neighbours.

questions.question: A hospital wants to (a) estimate how many days a patient will stay and (b) flag whether a patient will be readmitted within 30 days. For each goal, say whether it is a regression or a classification problem and explain why. Name one algorithm that could be used for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Length of stay is a regression problem: the target is a number of days, a continuous value that can take many possible values. Linear regression could be used.

(b) Readmission within 30 days is a classification problem, specifically binary: the target is one of two fixed categories (readmitted or not). Logistic regression, a decision tree or kNN could be used.

Both are supervised, because past patients come with known outcomes (labels).
rubric: Identifies (a) as regression and gives the reason: a continuous numeric target
Identifies (b) as classification (binary) and gives the reason: a fixed set of categories
Names a suitable algorithm for each, such as linear regression and logistic regression, kNN or a decision tree
Notes that both are supervised because the past outcomes act as labels

questions.question: A kNN classifier uses k = 3 to label the yellow star. Looking only at the solid ring, what class does it predict?
options: Red square, because two of the three nearest points are red squares
Blue circle, because blue circles are the most common class overall
Red square, because red squares are the class closest to the star
Blue circle, because the nearest single point to the star is blue
questions.explanation: kNN takes a majority vote among the k nearest labelled points: 2 squares against 1 circle.

questions.question: The same star is classified again with k = 7, using the dashed ring. What class does kNN predict now?
options: Red square, because the two closest points are still red squares
Blue circle, because five of the seven nearest points are blue circles
Red square, because a larger k always keeps the earlier answer
Blue circle, because the dashed ring is drawn in a lighter colour
questions.explanation: Changing the hyperparameter k changed the vote (2 squares and 5 circles), so the prediction flipped.

questions.question: In kNN, what is the usual effect of choosing k = 1?
options: The model averages over too many points, so it tends to underfit
The model ignores the training labels, so it tends to cluster
The model follows individual noisy points, so it tends to overfit
The model fits a straight line, so it tends to be a regression
questions.explanation: With k = 1 a single odd training point decides the answer nearby: low bias, high variance.

questions.question: In kNN, what is the usual effect of choosing a very large k, close to the size of the training set?
options: The vote is dominated by a single point, so the model tends to overfit
The vote is split evenly among classes, so the model always scores 50%
The vote is dropped completely, so the model starts to cluster the data
The vote is dominated by the biggest class, so the model tends to underfit
questions.explanation: A huge k smooths away local structure: high bias, low variance.

questions.question: How does a decision tree reach a prediction for a new example?
options: It follows a series of questions about feature values down the tree to a final class
It averages the answers of the k closest training examples to the new one
It moves a set of centres around until each example belongs to a group
It multiplies each feature by a learned weight and adds up the results
questions.explanation: Each decision node tests one feature (for example, is the commute under 30 minutes?). The leaf reached gives the class.

questions.question: What is a random forest?
options: A model made of many clusters whose centres are averaged
A model made of many decision trees whose predictions are combined
A model made of many neighbours whose labels are counted
A model made of many layers whose weights are adjusted
questions.explanation: Combining many trees is usually more reliable than relying on one tree.

questions.question: Plot A shows points around a rising line and Plot B shows two groups split by a boundary. Which pairing is right?
options: Plot A is classification (a category is predicted) and Plot B is regression (a number is predicted)
Plot A is regression (a category is predicted) and Plot B is clustering (a number is predicted)
Plot A is regression (a number is predicted) and Plot B is classification (a category is predicted)
Plot A is clustering (a number is predicted) and Plot B is classification (a category is predicted)
questions.explanation: A line through points predicts a continuous value (regression). A boundary between labelled groups assigns a category (classification).

questions.question: What is clustering?
options: Predicting a category for an example from a set of labelled ones
Predicting a number for an example from a set of labelled ones
Choosing actions for an agent from the rewards its environment gives
Grouping unlabelled examples so that similar ones end up together
questions.explanation: Clustering is the main example of unsupervised learning: no labels are given and the algorithm finds the groups.

questions.question: Clustering belongs to which family of machine learning?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Deep learning only
questions.explanation: Clustering finds structure in data that has no labels.

questions.question: What does the hyperparameter k mean in k-means?
options: The number of neighbours that vote on the label of a new example
The number of clusters you want the algorithm to find
The number of times that the algorithm repeats its training loop
The number of features that each example in the dataset has
questions.explanation: In k-means you choose k up front. (In kNN, k is a different thing: the number of neighbours.)

questions.question: What is a centroid in k-means?
options: The label of a cluster, which the algorithm is given before it starts
The farthest point in a cluster, which the algorithm uses as the boundary
The centre of a cluster, which the algorithm keeps moving to fit the data
The number of points in a cluster, which the algorithm uses to rank clusters
questions.explanation: Each centroid represents the centre of one cluster.

questions.question: How does k-means begin?
options: It reads the labels to place a centroid in each class
It places every example in a single large cluster
It asks the user to mark the centre of each cluster
It places k centroids at random positions
questions.explanation: The initial centroid positions are random; the algorithm then improves them.

questions.question: After the centroids are placed, what does k-means do over time?
options: It assigns points to the nearest centroid and moves each centroid toward the centre of its points
It assigns points to the farthest centroid and moves each centroid away from its own points
It assigns points to a random centroid and keeps the centroids where they were first placed
It assigns points to the label they were given and moves the centroids to match those labels
questions.explanation: These two steps repeat until the centroids settle on the actual cluster centres.

questions.question: You run k-means with k = 4 on customer data. How many clusters will the algorithm return?
options: Two
Four
However many labels the data has
Whatever number gives the best accuracy
questions.explanation: k is the number of clusters you ask for.

questions.question: k-means needs labelled examples in order to work.
questions.explanation: k-means is unsupervised. It only needs the features.

questions.question: In k-means, you choose the value of k before training.
questions.explanation: k is a hyperparameter set by the person, not learned by the algorithm.

questions.question: Which is a good use of clustering?
options: Predicting the price of a house from its size and location
Deciding whether a photograph contains a dog or does not
Finding natural groups of customers when no group names exist
Training a character to win a game by trial and error
questions.explanation: With no predefined groups, clustering lets the data suggest them. The others are regression, classification and reinforcement learning.

questions.question: Two runs of k-means on the same data, with the same k, can end up with different clusters. What is the most likely reason?
options: The labels are shuffled by the algorithm each time that it runs
The value of k is changed by the algorithm as it learns more
The data is deleted by the algorithm once a cluster is found
The starting positions of the centroids are chosen at random
questions.explanation: Random starting centroids can lead the algorithm to settle in different places.

questions.question: Match each k-means term to its meaning.

pairs.right: How many clusters to look for

questions.question: What is a parameter of a model?
options: A configuration option for the training algorithm that the engineer picks beforehand
A variable inside the model that the training algorithm sets by learning from data
A column in the dataset that describes each example and is fed to the model
A measure of how many of the model's predictions turned out to be correct
questions.explanation: Parameters are learned during training (for example the weights in a regression).

questions.question: What is a hyperparameter?
options: A variable inside the model that the training algorithm learns by itself
A feature in the dataset that has been scaled to lie between zero and one
A configuration of the training algorithm that we set ourselves
A label in the dataset that tells the model what the right answer is
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are set by us before training; parameters are set by the training algorithm.

questions.question: Who or what sets the value of a model's parameters?
options: The engineer, before training begins
The user, once the model is deployed
The labels, which are copied into the model
The training algorithm, as it learns from the data
questions.explanation: Parameters are trained; hyperparameters are chosen by the person.

questions.question: Who or what sets the value of a hyperparameter?
options: The person building the model
The training algorithm, as it learns
The test data, after training
The model, as it predicts
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are configuration choices made by us.

questions.question: Which of these is a hyperparameter?
options: The position of each centroid at the end of k-means
The number of clusters k in k-means
The slope that linear regression learns from the data
The label of each example in a training set
questions.explanation: k is chosen by us. The final centroid positions and a learned slope are parameters that the algorithm finds.

questions.question: Which of these is a parameter?
options: The number of neighbours that kNN consults for each new example
The maximum depth that is allowed for a decision tree
The slope and intercept that a line-fitting algorithm finds
The number of clusters that k-means is told to produce
questions.explanation: The slope and intercept are learned from data. The others are chosen by us before training.

questions.question: Hyperparameters are learned automatically from the training data.
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are set by us. Parameters are the values learned from the data.

questions.question: The positions of the centroids in k-means are parameters, because the algorithm moves them as it trains.
questions.explanation: Centroid positions are learned during training. The number of centroids, k, is the hyperparameter.

questions.question: Match each item to whether it is a parameter or a hyperparameter.

pairs.right: Hyperparameter: chosen by us before training
Parameter: moved by the algorithm during training
Parameter: found from the training data
Hyperparameter: a setting we configure

questions.question: Explain the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter. Use k-means to give one example of each, and say who or what sets each one.
questions.modelAnswer:
Parameters are variables inside the model that must be trained or optimised. The training algorithm sets them as it learns from the data. Hyperparameters are configuration settings for the training algorithm, and we set them ourselves before training begins.

In k-means, the hyperparameter is k, the number of clusters we ask the algorithm to find, and we choose it. The parameters are the centroid positions: they start at random and are moved by the algorithm until they sit at the actual cluster centres.
rubric: Defines a parameter as an internal variable trained or set by the training algorithm
Defines a hyperparameter as a configuration of the training algorithm set by us
Gives k as the k-means hyperparameter
Gives the centroid positions as the k-means parameters

questions.question: How is accuracy calculated?
options: The number of wrong predictions divided by the total number of samples
The number of correct predictions divided by the number of wrong predictions
The number of samples in the test set divided by the size of the whole dataset
The number of correct predictions divided by the total number of samples
questions.explanation: Accuracy = correct / total.

questions.question: A model makes 80 correct predictions out of 100 test samples. What is its accuracy?
A classifier predicts 45 of 60 samples correctly. What is its accuracy?
A model gets 18 predictions wrong out of 200 samples. What is its accuracy?
questions.explanation: It got 182 right: 182 / 200 = 0.91. The 9% is its error rate.

questions.question: What is a confusion matrix?
options: A list that shows each feature next to the weight it was given
A chart that shows how accuracy changes as training goes on
A table that shows which hyperparameters were tried and when
A grid that compares the actual classes with the predicted classes
questions.explanation: Rows and columns hold actual versus predicted classes, so you can see where the model gets confused.

questions.question: In a confusion matrix, where do the correct predictions appear?
options: On the diagonal, where the actual and predicted classes agree
Off the diagonal, where the actual and predicted classes differ
In the first row, where the first class is the one being counted
In the last column, where the totals for every class are written
questions.explanation: Cells where predicted equals actual are the correct ones.

questions.question: A confusion matrix for cats and dogs shows 40 cats called cats, 10 cats called dogs, 5 dogs called cats and 45 dogs called dogs. What is the accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct = 40 + 45 = 85 out of 100 total, which is 85%.

questions.question: A cat-and-dog classifier's confusion matrix has a cell with 10 cats that the model labelled as dogs. What does that cell represent?
options: Dogs that the model wrongly classified as cats
Cats that the model correctly classified as cats
Cats that the model wrongly classified as dogs
Dogs that the model correctly classified as dogs
questions.explanation: Off-diagonal cells are mistakes: actual cat, predicted dog.

questions.question: Accuracy is the number of wrong predictions divided by the total number of samples.
questions.explanation: That would be the error rate. Accuracy uses the correct predictions.

questions.question: A confusion matrix shows more detail than accuracy alone, because it shows which classes get mistaken for which.
questions.explanation: Accuracy is one number. The matrix shows where the mistakes happen.

questions.question: Using the confusion matrix shown (rows are the actual class, columns the predicted class), what is the accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct = 40 + 45 = 85 of 100 samples.

questions.question: What does generalization mean in machine learning?
options: How many different kinds of problem a model can be applied to without retraining
How quickly a model can be trained on a very large training set
How well a model performs on new examples that were not in its training set
How closely a model reproduces the answers for its own training examples
questions.explanation: A model that generalizes extends what it learned to unseen data.

questions.question: What is overfitting?
options: The model is too simple to capture the complexity that is in the data
The model is given too few examples for the algorithm to start training
The model is trained for so short a time that the parameters never change
The model memorizes the training set instead of learning the pattern behind it
questions.explanation: An overfit model matches the training data very closely but does not carry over to new data.

questions.question: What is underfitting?
options: The model is too simple to capture the complexity of the data
The model memorizes the training set instead of learning the pattern in it
The model gets perfect results on the training set and poor results on new data
The model is trained with so many examples that it can no longer improve
questions.explanation: An underfit model fails to capture the pattern even in the training data.

questions.question: Which pair of symptoms points to overfitting?
options: Low training accuracy and low test accuracy
High training accuracy and low test accuracy
Low training accuracy and high test accuracy
High training accuracy and high test accuracy
questions.explanation: A big gap between training and test performance means the model memorized the training set.

questions.question: A model scores 99% on its training data and 62% on its test data. What is the most likely problem?
options: Underfitting, and its bias is too high
Underfitting, and its variance is too high
Overfitting, and its variance is too high
Overfitting, and its bias is too high
questions.explanation: Great on training, poor on test: overfitting, which goes with high variance and low bias.

questions.question: A model scores 55% on its training data and 54% on its test data. What is the most likely problem?
options: Overfitting, and its bias is too high
Overfitting, and its variance is too high
Underfitting, and its variance is too high
Underfitting, and its bias is too high
questions.explanation: Poor on both: the model is too simple, which means high bias.

questions.question: Which combination describes an overfit model?
options: High variance and low bias
High bias and low variance
High bias and high variance
Low bias and low variance
questions.explanation: Overfit models are too sensitive to the training data (high variance) and fit it closely (low bias).

questions.question: Which combination describes an underfit model?
options: High variance and low bias
High bias and low variance
High variance and high bias
Low variance and low bias
questions.explanation: Underfit models make strong, simple assumptions (high bias) and change little with the data (low variance).

questions.question: What does training accuracy measure?
options: How accurate the model is on data it has never seen before
How accurate the model was before any training had been done
How accurate the model is on the data it was trained with
How accurate the model is once the hyperparameters are changed
questions.explanation: Training accuracy comes from the training data.

questions.question: What does test accuracy measure?
options: How accurate the model is on the data it learned from
How accurate the model was when training first started
How accurate the model is on the labels it is given
How accurate the model is on data held back from training
questions.explanation: Test accuracy shows how well the model generalizes to unseen examples.

questions.question: Why do we keep a separate test set that the model never trains on?
options: To measure how well the model works on examples it has not memorized
To give the model extra examples when the training set runs out
To let the model correct the labels of its training examples
To make the training run faster by reducing the data it reads
questions.explanation: Performance on training data alone cannot reveal overfitting; unseen data can.

questions.question: A model with very high training accuracy is guaranteed to perform well on new data.
questions.explanation: It may have memorized the training set. Test accuracy shows how well it generalizes.

questions.question: Low training accuracy means the model is underfitting, whether the test accuracy is low or high.
questions.explanation: If the model cannot even do well on the data it trained on, it is too simple: high bias.

questions.question: An overfit model has high bias and low variance.
questions.explanation: Overfit models have high variance and low bias. Underfit models have high bias and low variance.

questions.question: Match each result to the diagnosis.

pairs.left: High training accuracy, low test accuracy
pairs.right: Overfit: variance too high

pairs.left: Low training accuracy, low test accuracy
pairs.right: Underfit: bias too high

pairs.left: High training accuracy, high test accuracy
pairs.right: Generalizes well
Overfit

questions.question: A data scientist trains a model and reports 97% accuracy on the training data but only 68% on the test data. (a) Name the problem. (b) Describe it in terms of bias and variance. (c) Explain what the two accuracies tell you about generalization.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The model is overfitting: it has memorized the training set rather than learning the underlying pattern.

(b) An overfit model has high variance and low bias. It fits the training data very closely, but its predictions change a lot with the particular examples it saw, so it does not carry over.

(c) Generalization is how well the model does on unseen examples, and the test accuracy measures that. The large gap between 97% on training and 68% on test shows it generalizes poorly. High training accuracy alone says nothing about new data.
rubric: Names the problem as overfitting
States high variance and low bias
Explains that test accuracy measures generalization to unseen data
Points out that the large gap between training and test accuracy is the evidence

questions.question: Compare overfitting and underfitting. For each, give the training and test accuracy pattern, say whether bias or variance is too high, and say what the model has failed to do.
questions.modelAnswer:
Overfitting: training accuracy is high but test accuracy is low. Variance is too high (and bias is low). The model has memorized the training set instead of learning the pattern, so it fails to generalize to unseen examples.

Underfitting: training accuracy is low, and test accuracy is also low (or at best not high). Bias is too high (and variance is low). The model is too simple and does not capture the complexity of the data, so it fails even on the training set.
rubric: Overfit: high training and low test accuracy, with high variance
Underfit: low training accuracy, with high bias
Says an overfit model memorizes the training set and fails to generalize
Says an underfit model is too simple to capture the complexity of the data

questions.question: Each plot fits a curve to the same points. Which plot shows overfitting?
options: Plot B, where the line misses the shape of the points
Plot A, where the curve chases every single point
Plot C, where the curve follows the overall trend
None of them, because every plot reaches the points
questions.explanation: A curve that wiggles through every point memorizes noise: high variance, low bias.

questions.question: Each plot fits a curve to the same points. Which plot shows underfitting?
options: Plot A, where the curve follows the overall trend of the points
Plot B, where the curve bends to touch every one of the points
Plot C, where a straight line cannot follow the curved pattern
All three, because none of the curves is exactly on every point
questions.explanation: A line that is too simple for the data misses the pattern: high bias, low variance.

questions.question: Which plot shows the model most likely to generalize well to new points?
options: Plot A, which stays simple and ignores the curve in the data
Plot B, which touches each point in the training data
Plot A and Plot B, which are the two extremes of fitting
Plot C, which follows the trend without chasing noise
questions.explanation: The smooth curve captures the pattern and ignores the noise.

questions.question: A model's curve passes through every training point, as in the plot. What will probably happen on new data?
options: Training error is tiny but test error is large, because the model has high variance
Training error is large and test error is large, because the model has high bias
Training error is large but test error is tiny, because the model has high variance
Training error is tiny and test error is tiny, because the model has low bias
questions.explanation: The curve memorized the training points, including their noise.

questions.question: A straight line is fitted to the U-shaped points shown. Which statement describes the model?
options: High variance and low bias, because the line changes with every point
High bias and low variance, because the line is too simple for the data
High bias and high variance, because the line misses most of the points
Low bias and low variance, because the line is smooth and simple
questions.explanation: Too simple a model underfits: it is wrong in a consistent way (bias) and changes little with the data.

options: Underfitting, so bias is too high
Underfitting, so variance is too high
Overfitting, so variance is too high
A good fit, so bias and variance are both low
questions.explanation: Very high training accuracy with much lower test accuracy means the model memorized the training set.

questions.question: Which order correctly lists the main stages of training and checking a supervised model?
options: Prepare the data, train the model on the training set, then test it on the test set
Train the model on the test set, prepare the data, then check it on the training set
Test the model on the test set, prepare the data, then train it on the training set
Prepare the data, test the model on the training set, then train it on the test set
questions.explanation: Prepare (gather, choose features and target, split), train, then evaluate on data the model has not seen.

questions.question: Why is the data split into a training set and a test set before the model is fitted?
options: So the model can learn each example twice and remember it more reliably
So the model can later be scored on examples it did not learn from
So the model can skip the labels and look for groups in the test examples
So the model can set its own hyperparameters from the test examples
questions.explanation: A score on unseen data is the only honest measure of generalization.

questions.question: In a table of house data, you want to predict the sale price. What is the 'identify features and target' step?
options: Choosing the output columns (such as floor area) and the one column to hide (the price)
Choosing the rows used for training (such as the cheapest) and the rows kept for testing
Choosing the input columns (such as floor area) and the one column to predict (the price)
Choosing the algorithm to use (such as a line) and the number of clusters to look for
questions.explanation: Features are the inputs; the target is what the model is trained to predict.

questions.question: What happens in the 'fit' step of the process?
options: The training algorithm learns the model's hyperparameters from the test data
The training algorithm learns the model's labels from the training features
The training algorithm learns the model's accuracy from the unseen examples
The training algorithm learns the model's parameters from the training data
questions.explanation: Fitting (training) is where parameters are set by the algorithm. Hyperparameters are chosen by us beforehand.

questions.question: After a model is fitted, which data should be used to check its accuracy?
options: The test set, because the model never saw those examples during training
The training set, because the model learned those examples most thoroughly
The full dataset, because it contains the most examples of every kind
The feature columns, because they are the part the model was given
questions.explanation: Scoring on the training set would reward memorization.

questions.question: A dataset has 1,000 labelled rows. Which split is typical for supervised learning?
options: About 200 rows to train and 800 rows to test
About 800 rows to train and 200 rows to test
About 500 rows to train and 500 rows to test
About 995 rows to train and 5 rows to test
questions.explanation: Usually 70-80% of the data trains the model and 20-30% is held back to test it.

questions.question: You hold back 25% of 400 labelled rows as the test set. How many rows are left to train on?
questions.explanation: 25% of 400 is 100 test rows, which leaves 300 for training.

questions.question: In a typical split, the larger share of the data goes to the training set.
questions.explanation: Roughly 70-80% trains the model and 20-30% tests it.

questions.question: A model should be tested on the same examples it was trained on.
questions.explanation: That hides overfitting. Test on a held-back set so the score reflects generalization.

questions.question: The data is split into training and test sets before the model is trained.
questions.explanation: The split comes first, so the test set stays unseen during fitting.

questions.question: Training a model on the training data is also called ____ the model. (one word)
questions.explanation: To fit (train) a model is to let the algorithm set its parameters from the training data.

questions.question: Match each step of the process to what happens in it.

pairs.right: Collect the examples the model will learn from
Pick the input variables and the variable to predict
Set aside a test set the model will not train on
Let the algorithm learn from the training set
Measure accuracy on the held-back examples

questions.question: Describe the basic process of training a machine learning model and checking that it works. List the main steps in order and say what happens in each.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Gather the data: collect the examples (rows) the model will learn from.

2. Identify the features and the target: choose the input variables (features) and the one variable to predict (the target, or label).

3. Split the data into a training set and a test set, so some examples are held back from training.

4. Choose an algorithm and set its hyperparameters, then fit (train) the model on the training set. The algorithm sets the parameters.

5. Test the model on the test set and compute its accuracy. Compare training and test accuracy to see whether it generalizes, or is overfitting or underfitting. If it is poor, adjust and repeat.
rubric: Gather or collect the data
Identifies the features and the target variable
Splits the data into training and test sets
Fits or trains the model on the training set
Tests the model on the held-back test set and measures accuracy
Steps are in a sensible order (the test set is not used for training)

questions.question: Explain, in three main points, how a supervised machine learning model is built and evaluated. For each point, say what is done and why it matters.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Prepare the data. Gather the examples, identify the features (inputs) and the target (what to predict), and split the data into a training set and a test set. The split matters because it keeps some examples unseen.

2. Train the model. Choose an algorithm and its hyperparameters, then fit the model to the training set so the algorithm learns the parameters. This is where the model learns the pattern.

3. Evaluate the model. Test it on the test set and measure accuracy. This matters because it shows how well the model generalizes; a big gap between training and test accuracy means overfitting.
rubric: Point on preparing the data: gathering it, features and target, and the training/test split
Point on training: fitting the model to the training set
Point on evaluating: testing on unseen data and measuring accuracy
Gives a reason for the split or for testing on unseen data (generalization)
